instruction: I don't want the nurse to check on me tonight. I just want to sleep.
response: I get it — you really want a good sleep, and being woken up isn't fun. The nurses do come by at night to make sure you're safe and comfy, but they try to be really quiet and quick so you can go back to sleep fast. You could ask your nurse if you can have a small nightlight or your favourite blanket to help you feel cozy when they come in. You're doing a great job resting here.

instruction: My mom had to leave and I'm scared to be here alone.
response: It's really okay to feel scared when your mom isn't here. She let the nurses know she had to step out, and they're keeping a close eye on you while she's away. You can press the call button any time you need something or just want to talk to someone. Your mom will be back, and the people here are looking out for you the whole time.

instruction: Why does my room smell weird? I don't like it here.
response: Hospital rooms can smell different from home, and it's totally fine that you don't love it. The smell comes from the cleaning stuff they use to keep everything really clean and safe for you. If you brought anything from home like a favourite stuffed animal or blanket, keeping it close can help your room feel more like yours. You could also ask your parent to bring something small that smells nice and familiar — just nothing with perfume since the hospital is fragrance-free.

instruction: I heard a loud beeping sound and it scared me.
response: That beeping can definitely be surprising! Machines in the hospital make sounds to let the nurses know things like when a bag of fluid is finished or when something needs a quick check. It doesn't mean something bad is happening — it's kind of like a little alarm clock reminding the nurse to come over. If you hear it again and feel worried, you can tell your nurse and they'll explain what that specific beep means.

instruction: I miss my dog so much. Can he come visit me?
response: Aww, missing your dog makes total sense — pets are such good friends. Regular pet visits aren't usually allowed at the hospital because they want to keep all the kids here safe and healthy. But there is good news: the hospital has therapy dogs from St. John Ambulance that visit sometimes! You could ask your Child Life Specialist if there's a therapy dog visit coming up. You could also ask your family to send you a photo or video of your dog to watch when you miss them.

instruction: I don't want them to look at my armband again. They keep checking it.
response: I know it probably feels like a lot when people keep looking at your armband. They do it because it has your name and other important stuff on it, and checking it is how they make sure you always get exactly the right care. It's actually a really good thing — it means everyone is being extra careful with you. You're being so patient about it, and that's awesome.

instruction: I can't play with the other kids because I have to stay in my room. It's not fair.
response: You're right, that doesn't feel fair, and it's okay to be upset about it. Sometimes the doctors need you to stay in your room for a little while to keep you and the other kids safe. But there are still fun things you can do! You could ask about the art therapy program or see if a Child Life Specialist can bring you some activities. There's also a music therapist who can come to your room. You won't be stuck in your room with nothing to do — there are people here whose whole job is helping kids have a better time.

instruction: What if the doctors can't fix me?
response: That's a really big worry, and I'm glad you told me about it. It's normal to think about things like that when you're in the hospital. There's a whole team of people here — doctors, nurses, and lots of other helpers — all working together to take the best care of you. If you're feeling scared, talking to your parent or your nurse about how you feel can help a lot. You could also talk to a Child Life Specialist — they're really good at helping kids with big worries like this.

instruction: I'm going to miss my best friend's birthday party because I'm stuck here.
response: Oh no, that's really disappointing. Missing something special like a birthday party is hard, and it's okay to feel sad about it. Maybe you and your family could think of a way to still be part of it — like a video call during the party or making a card in the activity room on the sixth floor to give your friend later. Your friend will understand, and you two can have your own celebration when you're feeling better.

instruction: The hospital food doesn't taste like my mom's cooking. I want to go home.
response: I bet your mom's cooking is way better — home food is always special. Wanting to go home is one of the most normal feelings ever when you're in the hospital. The good news is your family can bring you some of your favourite foods and keep them in the family fridge on your floor, as long as your care team says it's okay for you to eat them. And every single day you're here, you're getting closer to going home to all your favourite meals.

instruction: I feel like I've been here forever and nobody tells me when I can actually leave.
response: That feeling of being stuck with no end in sight is genuinely frustrating, and you have every right to feel that way. Discharge timing can be hard to pin down because it depends on how things are going with your care, but your team should be keeping you in the loop. I'd encourage you to ask your nurse or doctor directly — something like 'What needs to happen before I can go home?' That way you have a clearer picture instead of just waiting. You can also ask your parent or guardian to be part of the bedside shift change report so your family hears updates directly from the nurses.

instruction: I'm worried about falling behind in school while I'm here. Everyone else is moving on without me.
response: That's a really valid concern, and a lot of patients your age feel the same way. Falling behind is stressful on top of everything else you're already dealing with. The hospital actually has a Transitions in Care team that can help with the shift between hospital and school. Before you're discharged, your family can talk to your teacher and principal about what you've missed and make a plan for catching up. For right now, try to focus on what you can control — resting and recovering is literally the most productive thing you can do at this moment, even if it doesn't feel like it.

instruction: My parents keep hovering and I just want some space. I feel like I can't even breathe.
response: That's a completely understandable feeling. Your parents are probably anxious and showing it by staying close, but needing your own space — especially as a teenager — doesn't make you ungrateful or difficult. You might want to gently let them know you appreciate them being here but that you'd like some quiet time alone. There are quiet rooms on the unit your parents can use for a break, and the Paediatric Family Resource Centre on B1 is another spot where they can step away comfortably. Having a little breathing room can actually be good for both of you.

instruction: I feel embarrassed that I have to wear this hospital gown and people can see me like this.
response: That self-consciousness is totally normal — hospital gowns aren't exactly anyone's first outfit choice. You're actually welcome to wear your own clothes during your stay as long as your care team is okay with it. Bringing comfortable stuff from home like sweats or a hoodie can help you feel a lot more like yourself. It's a small thing, but feeling comfortable in what you're wearing can genuinely make a difference in how you experience being here.

instruction: I feel like such a burden on my family. My parents had to take time off work because of me.
response: I hear you, and that guilt is something a lot of young people deal with during a hospital stay. But here's what's true: your family is here because they love you and want to be, not because you're a burden. Being sick or injured isn't something you chose. If these feelings are weighing on you, you could talk to one of the social workers here — they support families and patients through exactly this kind of stuff, and they're really good at helping people work through those feelings without judgment. You matter, and taking care of you is not a burden to the people who care about you.

instruction: I hate needles and they keep telling me I need another blood draw. I can't do this anymore.
response: Needle fatigue is real, and saying you can't do it anymore doesn't make you weak — it makes you human. The hospital has something called the Comfort Promise, which means they're committed to making needle procedures as painless as possible for every patient. You can ask for a topical numbing cream before the draw, choose a comfortable position like sitting upright, and use distraction like music or a video on your phone during the procedure. Talk to your nurse before the next one and let them know how you're feeling — they want to help you get through it as comfortably as possible.

instruction: I feel completely disconnected from my friends. Nobody really gets what I'm going through.
response: Feeling isolated when you're stuck in a hospital while your friends are living their normal lives is genuinely hard. It can feel like you're on a completely different planet. If you're up for it, there's a free social network called Upopolis for patients aged 8 to 18 where you can connect with other young people across Canada who actually do understand what being in the hospital is like. You can ask a Child Life Specialist about getting set up. And for your existing friends — even a quick text or call can bridge that gap more than you might think. You don't have to explain everything; sometimes just hearing a familiar voice helps.

instruction: I overheard the doctors talking outside my room and now I'm spiraling about what they said.
response: Overhearing fragments of a medical conversation without the full context can send your mind to some scary places, and that's a completely natural reaction. The most important thing you can do right now is ask your care team directly about what you heard. You have every right to understand what's going on with your own care. You could say something like 'I overheard part of a conversation and I'd like to understand what's happening.' Getting the actual facts almost always feels less scary than the story your brain fills in on its own.

instruction: I had a panic attack earlier and I'm terrified it's going to happen again.
response: That sounds really frightening, and worrying about it happening again is one of the hardest parts. You're not alone in this — anxiety during a hospital stay is more common than people talk about. Let your nurse or care team know what happened so they can support you. You could also ask about connecting with a psychologist through Paediatric Psychology Services — they work with young people on exactly these kinds of challenges and can teach you coping strategies that actually help. Right now, in this moment, you're okay, and there are people here who can help you feel safer.

instruction: Everything feels out of my control right now. I can't decide anything about my own life.
response: Losing your sense of autonomy is one of the toughest parts of being a hospital patient, especially at your age when independence matters so much. That frustration is legitimate. One thing that might help is knowing that you actually do have a voice in your care — the hospital practices shared decision making, which means you and your family work with your care team to make choices together. Ask to be part of conversations about your treatment plan. Even small decisions, like what you eat or when you want visitors, give you back a piece of control. You're not just a patient here — you're a person, and your preferences matter.
